stories.title: Le train de 7h12
stories.summary: A man misses the same train twice in one week, and the second time is deliberate.

lines.en: The old man closed the door without a sound.

notes.note: «vieux homme» would put the «eu» sound straight against the «o» of «homme», which French avoids, so the word changes shape to «vieil». Say it out loud and you can hear why: vieil-homme runs together, vieux-homme stumbles.

You'd expect «a fermé» here, and in speech that's exactly what you'd get. This is written storytelling, so the verb takes its written-only form, «ferma». It means the same thing; it just sounds like a book rather than a conversation.

lines.en: She hadn't heard him leave.

notes.note: This «l'» is «le», meaning him — her husband. «Le avait» is unsayable, so the vowel drops out and the word leans onto the next one.
The two halves close around «avait», leaving «entendu partir» outside on the right. Watch where «pas» lands: after the small verb that carries the tense, not after the verb that carries the meaning.

«avait entendu» is a step further back than the rest of the story. He had already gone; her not-hearing happened before that. French marks that extra step back the same way English does, with «had» plus the participle.

lines.en: Outside, it was still raining.

notes.note: Nothing is doing the raining here. This «il» is a placeholder, the way English says "it's raining" without meaning anything by "it".

lines.en: He walked to the station, his hands in his pockets.

notes.note: «à la gare» on its own would just say where he ended up. «jusqu'à» adds the whole distance — he walked the entire way, no bus, no lift.
English needs "his hands, his pockets" here; French says «les». They're obviously his hands, so marking it would be fussy, and «ses mains dans ses poches» sounds like someone learning the language.

lines.en: The 7:12 train was leaving without him, like every Tuesday.

notes.note: «partait» leaves the departure open — the train pulling out, the thing that happens every Tuesday, the background he's standing in. Compare the last line of the story, where the same train «partit». That one is finished.
After «sans» you can't use the little «le» that hides in front of a verb. The standalone form «lui» is what goes after a preposition, and it's the same word you'd use alone: «Lui ? Jamais.»

lines.en: He'd stopped at the corner for no reason, and that had been enough.

notes.note: Plain «arrêter» means stopping something else — a car, a thief. To come to a halt yourself you stop yourself, so the verb needs its «se»: «s'arrêter». And once that «se» is there the past is built with «être», never «avoir».

lines.en: For forty years he had taken that train every morning.

notes.note: «Pendant» is for a stretch of time that's over and done with. The forty years finished; he's retired now. If he still took the train it would be «depuis quarante ans».

lines.en: He knew the name of every station between his house and Rouen.

notes.note: Knowing the names wasn't an event with a start and a finish — it was simply true of him. States like this take «connaissait», not «connut». «Il connut» would mean he found out, in one moment.
There's no French word for "home" as a place you go to. «chez» plus a person means at or to that person's place, so «chez lui» is his house, his flat, wherever he lives.

lines.en: Now there was no office, no colleagues, nobody waiting for him.

notes.note: «pas» isn't the only word that finishes a negation. «plus» in this position means not any more — the office existed once and doesn't now. Read it aloud with a silent «s»; that's usually what tells it apart from «plus» meaning more.
You'd expect «un bureau». After a negation the article collapses to a bare «de», so «un bureau» becomes «plus de bureau» — the same thing happens to «des collègues» right after it.
English puts "-ing" after the preposition: nobody waiting. French can't do that, so «pour» is followed by the plain «attendre», with the «l'» meaning him tucked in front of it.

lines.en: But on Tuesdays he set out all the same.

notes.note: «mardi» on its own would mean one particular Tuesday. Adding «le» turns it into every Tuesday, the standing arrangement — which is the whole point of this sentence.

lines.en: He'd have a coffee across from his old office, walk for an hour, then come home.

notes.note: Three verbs in a row, all in the same form, because none of them is a single event. This is what he did every Tuesday, the shape of the day rather than one particular day. English reaches for "he'd" to say the same thing.
In front of the noun, «ancien» means former — the office he used to work in. Put it after and «un bureau ancien» would be a piece of antique furniture, which is a very different sentence.

lines.en: His wife had never asked him any questions.

notes.note: «lui» here means to him, and it sits in front of the verb group where English puts it after: asked him. Once you have a pronoun instead of a full name, it moves left and stays there.

lines.en: That morning he came home at eleven, his shoes soaked.

notes.note: Everything before this line was the routine. This one verb changes form, and that alone tells you the routine broke — one particular morning, one specific arrival, eleven o'clock instead of the evening.
French can hang a bare noun phrase on the end of a sentence to describe the state someone is in, with no verb and no "with". It's the same move as «les mains dans les poches» in the fourth line.

lines.en: His wife looked up from her paper.

notes.note: «ses yeux» would be odd here — whose eyes could they be? French leaves the ownership implied and uses «les», exactly as it did with his hands and his pockets.

lines.en: He told her he'd missed the train.

notes.note: English lets you drop "that" — he told her he'd missed it. French never does; «qu'» has to be there. And since «il» starts with a vowel, «que» loses its own vowel and becomes «qu'».

lines.en: She didn't ask him which one.

notes.note: "Which one" is a single word in French, and it carries the gender and number of what it stands for. It's standing in for «le train» here, so it comes out masculine and singular: «lequel».

lines.en: The following Friday he got up before the alarm.

notes.note: «lever» is to lift something. What he lifts is himself, so the «se» is doing real work: «se lever» is how French says get up. Drop it and you've said he lifted something, and the sentence stops making sense.

lines.en: It had stopped raining.
He got to the station ten minutes early.

notes.note: «arriver» takes «à» before a place, always — you can't arrive a station in French any more than you can in English. The «à» is part of the verb's habit, not something you choose.

lines.en: The train was already there, doors open.

notes.note: «ouvert» grows an «e» for the feminine «portes» and an «s» because there are several — «ouvertes». You can't hear the difference when it's read aloud, but leaving it off looks wrong on the page.

lines.en: He sat down on a bench, his ticket in his hand.

notes.note: «son» doesn't tell you the owner is male — it tells you «billet» is a masculine word. His wife's ticket would also be «son billet» — and «son journal», seven lines back, was hers for exactly the same reason.

lines.en: A woman asked him if he was getting on.

notes.note: «si» meaning if normally keeps its vowel — «si elle montait» is fine. In front of «il» and «ils» only, it shortens to «s'», which is why this looks like the «s'» of a reflexive verb but isn't one.

lines.en: He shook his head.

notes.note: French says he made no with the head. There's no verb for shaking your head; «faire» plus «oui» or «non» covers both, and it's the ordinary everyday way to say it.

lines.en: The doors closed.

notes.note: Nobody is closing them, and «les portes fermèrent» would be wrong. The «se» is how French says a thing happens to itself when the doer is irrelevant — here, the doors close on their own schedule, which is rather the point.

lines.en: The 7:12 train left without him.

notes.note: Same train, same words, one letter of difference from the fifth line of the story. «partait» was a train in the act of leaving, every Tuesday. «partit» is one departure, complete, and he watched it happen.

lines.en: He walked home through the back streets, taking his time.

notes.note: English would say "without hurrying". French puts the plain infinitive after «sans», and «se presser» keeps its «se» because what he isn't hurrying is himself.

lines.en: His wife was standing in the kitchen, and there were two cups on the table.

notes.note: Word for word this is "it there had", which is no help at all. Taken together the three words mean there was or there were — and unlike English, the phrase never changes for a plural. Two cups, still «il y avait».

lines.en: She'd been setting out two since Tuesday.

notes.note: «en» stands in for «des tasses» — of them. French won't let you say «elle mettait deux» and stop there; if you don't name the thing, «en» has to hold its place in front of the verb.
«depuis» plus this form of the verb is how French says something started back then and is still going. English needs a whole scaffolding — she'd been setting out — where French needs one preposition.

stories.title: Sous le même parapluie
stories.summary: A woman shares a stranger's umbrella one rainy morning, and it turns into a small daily habit.

lines.en: Léa lives on a small street, next to a bakery.

notes.note: «de» would run straight into «une», two vowel sounds with nothing between them, so it drops its own vowel and becomes «d'». You'll see the same move happen to «le» and «la» later in the story.

lines.en: Every morning, she buys bread and croissants before work.

notes.note: Léa isn't buying one specific, whole loaf — «pain» is masculine, so «de» plus «le» contracts to «du», and together they mean some bread, an amount with no number attached.
Same idea for the croissants: an unspecified number of them, so the plural partitive «des» does the job. English just says croissants and leaves the amount implied.

lines.en: She waits for the bus in front of the bakery.
There's always a man at the same stop, but she doesn't know his name.

notes.note: Nothing here literally means it, there, or has on its own — the three words work as one fixed phrase for there is. It's how the man at the stop gets introduced into the story.

lines.en: One Tuesday, it had been raining since morning.

notes.note: «depuis» plus this imparfait form, «pleuvait», says the rain had already been going on before this moment and was still happening then — not one downpour, but weather that was already the backdrop.

lines.en: Léa ran to the bus stop.

notes.note: The line before this one set the scene with «pleuvait» — imparfait, ongoing. This verb switches to passé composé because running to the stop is a single, finished action: she started, she arrived, done.
«à l'arrêt» alone would just name where she ended up. «jusqu'à» adds the whole distance she covered getting there — she ran the entire way.

lines.en: She looked for her umbrella in her bag, but it wasn't there.

notes.note: Searching her bag, «a cherché», is the event; the umbrella simply not being there is the state she found. That's why the two verbs sit in different tenses in the same sentence.

Two lines, two different things called «son» — «son parapluie» and now «son sac» — because both «parapluie» and «sac» are masculine words, not because two different people own them. It's always Léa's.

lines.en: She'd left it on the kitchen table.

notes.note: «l'» stands for the umbrella and sits right in front of «a», the helping verb. English puts it after the verb — left it — but French moves it left and keeps it there.

lines.en: The bus wasn't there yet.
The man raised his black umbrella above her.

notes.note: «de» meets «elle», another vowel start, and contracts the same way it did in the first line of the story — this time after the compound preposition «au-dessus», above.
After a preposition like «au-dessus de», French needs the standalone pronoun «elle», not a form that hides in front of a verb. It's the same slot «lui» fills after «sans» or «chez».

lines.en: "You don't have an umbrella?" he asked.

notes.note: Asked as a plain fact, this would be «un parapluie». Once «ne … pas» is in the sentence, the article shrinks to bare «de» — the same drop you'd see in a statement.
Flipping «il a» to make a question would give «a-il», two vowels colliding. French drops in a «t» that carries no meaning at all — it's only there to make the question sayable.

lines.en: "No, I forgot it," Léa replied, and she laughed.

notes.note: «le», standing for the umbrella, meets «ai» and loses its vowel the same way «de» and «que» do elsewhere in the story. Say «le ai» out loud and you'll hear why it can't stay whole.

lines.en: They stayed under the umbrella until the bus arrived.

notes.note: «rester» is one of the small set of verbs that build their past with «être» instead of «avoir». Because the subject is «ils», the participle picks up an «s»: «restés», the way an adjective would.
Same word, same job as the first time it appeared: not just where they end up, but the whole stretch of time they stood there, right up to the bus turning up.

lines.en: On the bus, they talked for the first time.

notes.note: «fois» is feminine, so the ordinal «premier» takes its feminine form, «première», with the extra «e». Say «premier fois» out loud in French and it sounds wrong before you can explain why.

lines.en: She learned his name was Thomas, and that he works near her place.

notes.note: English would happily drop that here: she learned he's called Thomas. French can't; «que» has to introduce what she learned, and it shortens to «qu'» because «il» starts with a vowel.
«chez elle» means at her place, near where she lives — there's no French word that just means home the way English has one, so «chez» plus the person does that job instead.

lines.en: Since that day, Léa never forgets her umbrella.

notes.note: That Tuesday marked a starting point, and the habit is still going now, so it's «depuis», not «pendant». If the habit had already ended, French would switch to «pendant ce jour-là».
«plus» here means not any more, not more — she used to forget it and now she doesn't. Read the sentence with a silent «s» on «plus» and that's the sense you want.

lines.en: She even brings a second one, for Thomas.

notes.note: «en» stands in for parapluies without naming it again — a second one of them. Leave it out and «elle apporte même un deuxième» is missing a piece; French won't let the sentence stand without it.

lines.en: It doesn't always rain, but she brings it anyway.

notes.note: Same empty «il» as the rain earlier in the story — nothing is doing the raining, the pronoun is just a placeholder the sentence needs to have a subject at all.
«pleut» is the only verb in the sentence, so that's what the negation wraps — no helping verb here to argue about, unlike the compound tenses earlier in the story.

lines.en: One morning, Thomas arrives with two coffees.
"For you," he says, "rain or not."
Now, they wait for the bus together, every morning.
And Léa doesn't walk home alone anymore when it rains.

notes.note: The same not any more as before, now about walking home alone rather than forgetting an umbrella — the routine that changed is different, but the grammar doing the work is identical.
«seul» adds an «e» to agree with Léa, who's «elle», not «il». Drop the «e» and the sentence would technically describe a man walking home alone.

rules.name: Verbs that need «à» before a place
rules.body:
Some French verbs come with a preposition attached, and you can't drop it even
when English has none. «arriver» is one: you always arrive **at**.

- Il arriva **à** la gare. — He reached the station.
- Elle est entrée **dans** la cuisine. — She entered the kitchen.
- Nous allons **à** Rouen. — We're going to Rouen.

Cities take «à», feminine countries take «en» (en France), masculine ones take
«au» (au Portugal).

rules.name: Adjectives match the noun in gender and number
rules.body:
An adjective takes an «e» for a feminine noun and an «s» for a plural, in
whatever order applies. You often can't hear it; you always have to write it.

- portes **ouvertes** — feminine and plural, so «-es».
- les chaussures **trempées** — same, and the participle behaves like an adjective.
- un banc **vert**, une porte **verte**, des portes **vertes**.

Adjectives already ending in «e» add only the «s»: «une rue calme», «des rues
calmes».

rules.name: Adjectives that change shape before a vowel
rules.body:
Three common adjectives have a third form used only in front of a masculine
noun starting with a vowel or a silent «h». It exists purely so the words don't
collide when you say them.

- vieux → **vieil** : un vieil homme, un vieil ami. But un vieux monsieur.
- beau → **bel** : un bel été. But un beau jardin.
- nouveau → **nouvel** : un nouvel appartement. But un nouveau bureau.

The feminine forms already end in a consonant sound — vieille, belle, nouvelle —
so they never need this and never change.

rules.name: Adjectives that change meaning when they move
rules.body:
Most French adjectives follow the noun. A few can go either side, and the side
changes what they mean — before the noun the sense is figurative, after it the
sense is literal.

- son **ancien** bureau (his former office) / un bureau **ancien** (an antique desk)
- un **grand** homme (a great man) / un homme **grand** (a tall man)
- mon **propre** livre (my own book) / un livre **propre** (a clean book)

The same list includes cher, pauvre, and dernier. When in doubt, put the
adjective after — that's where the plain meaning lives.

rules.name: A bare noun phrase tacked on to describe a state
rules.body:
French can end a sentence with a comma and a naked noun phrase — no verb, no
"with" — describing the state of the person or thing just mentioned.

- Il rentra, **les chaussures trempées**. — his shoes soaked.
- Le train était là, **portes ouvertes**. — doors open.
- Il s'assit, **son billet à la main**. — ticket in hand.

English needs "with" or a participle to do this. French needs nothing, which is
why it reads as compact and slightly literary.

rules.name: «le» where English says "my", "his", "her"
rules.body:
With parts of the body, and with clothes you're wearing, French uses the plain
definite article. Whose they are is obvious, so saying it would sound heavy.

- les mains dans **les** poches — his hands in his pockets.
- Elle leva **les** yeux. — She looked up (lifted her eyes).
- Il a mal à **la** tête. — His head hurts.

Use «son», «sa», «ses» here and a French reader hears a learner. Save the
possessives for things that could belong to somebody else.

rules.name: «chez» — at someone's place
rules.body:
«chez» has no English equivalent. It means at or to the home, shop, or world
of the person named after it, and it must be followed by a person, not a place.

- **chez** lui — at his place, home.
- Je vais **chez** le médecin. — To the doctor's.
- **chez** Renault — at Renault, as an employer.

You cannot say «chez la maison». For a building you use «à»: «à la maison».

rules.name: After a negation, «un» and «du» collapse to «de»
rules.body:
A negated verb strips the article down to a bare «de» (or «d'»). The thing
doesn't exist, so French stops marking how much of it there is.

- Il y a **un** bureau. → Il n'y a plus **de** bureau.
- Elle pose **des** questions. → Elle ne pose pas **de** questions.
- Je bois **du** café. → Je ne bois pas **de** café.

The definite article survives untouched: «je n'aime pas **le** café» — I don't
like coffee in general. And «être» is exempt: «ce n'est pas **un** train».

rules.name: «le mardi» means every Tuesday
rules.body:
A bare day name points at one particular day. Add «le» and it becomes a
routine — the same thing English does with a plural.

- **mardi**, il part à sept heures. — This coming Tuesday.
- **le** mardi, il part à sept heures. — On Tuesdays, as a rule.
- **le** matin, elle lit le journal. — In the mornings.

Same trick with «le soir», «le week-end», «l'été». Without the article you're
naming an occasion; with it, a habit.

rules.name: «pendant» and «depuis» — two kinds of "for"
rules.body:
English uses "for" for both. French splits them by whether the thing is over.

- **Pendant** quarante ans, il avait pris ce train. — Finished stretch.
- Il travaille ici **depuis** quarante ans. — Started then, still true.
- Elle en mettait deux **depuis** mardi. — Since Tuesday, still doing it.

The tense follows the choice. «depuis» goes with the present for something
still going on, or the imparfait inside a story — never the tense English uses
("has been"). «pendant» goes with a finished past.

rules.name: Small words drop their vowel before another vowel
rules.body:
A handful of one-syllable words lose their final vowel when the next word
begins with a vowel or a silent «h». The apostrophe is what's left of it. This
is not optional and not casual — writing the full form would be a mistake.

- le, la → **l'** : l'homme, l'avait entendu.
- de → **d'** : dix minutes d'avance.
- ne → **n'** : il n'y avait plus rien.
- que → **qu'** : il dit qu'il avait raté le train.

«l'» hides which word it came from, so «l'» can be the, him, or her, and only
the sentence tells you which.

rules.name: «si» shortens only before «il» and «ils»
rules.body:
«si» meaning if keeps its vowel almost everywhere. The single exception is in
front of «il» and «ils».

- Elle demanda **s'il** montait. — if he was getting on.
- Elle demanda **s'ils** montaient. — if they were.
- But: **si elle** montait, **si on** partait, **si un** train arrivait.

Because of this, «s'il» looks identical to the «s'» of «s'arrêter» and is a
completely different word. Check what follows: a pronoun subject means «if».

rules.name: The extra «-t-» that stops two vowels colliding
rules.body:
To ask a question, French can flip the verb and its subject: «il a» becomes
«a-t-il». «a» and «il» are both vowel sounds, and saying them back to back is
awkward, so a «t» gets inserted between them purely for the sound. It doesn't
mean anything on its own — it's only there to make the question sayable.

- Il **a** un parapluie. → **A-t-il** un parapluie ? — never «a-il».
- Elle **arrive**. → **Arrive-t-elle** demain ?
- Il **dit** vrai. → **Dit-il** vrai ? — «dit» already ends on a consonant
  sound, so no extra «-t-» is needed.

You only see this «-t-» after a verb form that ends in a vowel, like «-e» or
«-a». Once the verb already ends in a consonant, like «dit» or «part», the
subject just attaches directly.

rules.name: «faire» does the work of many English verbs
rules.body:
French leans on «faire» — to do, to make — where English has a specific verb.
These are set phrases; the pieces don't translate one by one.

- **faire non de la tête** — to shake one's head. Literally: to make no with the head.
- **faire la queue** — to queue.
- **faire attention** — to pay attention.
- Il **fait** froid. — It's cold.

Learn each as a block. Assembling them from the English is how you end up with
sentences no one says.

rules.name: «il y a» — there is, there are
rules.body:
Three words that only mean anything together. Word for word it's "it there
has", which is no help; take it as one block meaning there is or there are.

- **Il y a** deux tasses sur la table. — There are two cups.
- **Il y avait** plus personne. — There was no one left.
- **Il y a** trois ans — three years ago. Same phrase, time meaning.

It never becomes plural — «il y a deux tasses», never «ils y ont». Only the
tense of «avoir» changes: il y avait, il y aura, il y a eu.

rules.name: Imparfait or passé composé — background versus event
rules.body:
Both describe the past, and in speech that's the choice most people actually
have to make. The imparfait (**-ait**, **-aient**) paints the scene: what was
going on, what was already true. The passé composé (**avoir**/**être** plus a
participle) is the thing that happened — one event, with a start and a finish.

- Il **pleuvait** depuis le matin. Léa **a couru** jusqu'à l'arrêt. — The rain
  is the backdrop; the running is the thing that happened.
- Le bus **n'était pas** encore là. — Still the backdrop: a state, not an
  event.
- Elle **a cherché** son parapluie, mais il **n'était pas** là. — One search
  (event) inside one unchanging fact (state).

Ask yourself: is this the picture, or is this the next thing that happened?
The picture takes imparfait; the next thing takes passé composé.

rules.name: Imparfait or passé simple — the choice that carries the story
rules.body:
Both are past. The imparfait (-ait, -aient) is unfinished: the setting, the
habit, the state, what was going on. The passé simple — or the passé composé in
speech — is one completed event that moves the story forward.

- Il **pleuvait**. Il **ferma** la porte. — Rain all around; one closed door.
- Le train **partait** sans lui, comme chaque mardi. — The weekly pattern.
- Le train **partit** sans lui. — One departure, over.

Same verb, different frame. Ask whether you're describing the picture or
adding the next thing that happened.

rules.name: «jusqu'à» — all the way to
rules.body:
«à» tells you the destination. «jusqu'à» tells you the whole distance or
duration was covered — up to and including that point.

- Il marcha **jusqu'à** la gare. — He walked the entire way there.
- Elle a attendu **jusqu'à** midi. — Right up until noon.
- **jusqu'au** bout — all the way to the end. («à + le» contracts as usual.)

It behaves like «à» afterwards: «jusqu'au», «jusqu'aux», and «jusqu'en» before
a year or a month.

rules.name: «lequel» — which one
rules.body:
«quel» sits in front of a noun; «lequel» replaces the noun entirely and means
which one. It agrees with whatever it stands for.

- **Quel** train ? — Which train? → **Lequel** ? — Which one?
- masculine: lequel / lesquels — feminine: laquelle / lesquelles.
- Elle ne lui demanda pas **lequel**. — She didn't ask which one.

After «à» and «de» it contracts: «auquel», «duquel», «desquelles».

rules.name: Beyond «pas» — plus, jamais, rien, personne
rules.body:
«ne» is the constant; the second word chooses the meaning. Swap «pas» for
another and you get a different negative, in the same position.

- ne … **plus** — not any more. Il n'y avait **plus** de bureau.
- ne … **jamais** — never. Elle ne lui avait **jamais** posé de questions.
- ne … **rien** — nothing. Il ne dit **rien**.
- ne … **personne** — nobody. Il n'y avait **personne**.

Never combine them with «pas». «ne … plus» already contains the negation;
«ne pas plus» is not French.

rules.name: Negation wraps the conjugated verb
rules.body:
French negates with a pair: «ne» before the verb, «pas» after it. In compound
tenses the pair closes around the small verb that carries the tense, not around
the participle that carries the meaning.

- Je **ne** mange **pas**. — I'm not eating.
- Je **n'**ai **pas** mangé. — I haven't eaten. Never «je n'ai mangé pas».
- Elle **ne** l'avait **pas** entendu partir. — «pas» lands after «avait».

Object pronouns stay inside the sandwich too, tucked between «ne» and the verb:
«je **ne** le vois **pas**».

rules.name: Object pronouns go in front of the verb
rules.body:
Replace a noun with a pronoun and it moves to the left, in front of the verb
group. English keeps it after the verb; French almost never does.

- Elle ne **lui** avait jamais posé de questions. — asked **him**.
- Je **le** vois. — I see **him**.
- Il **nous** a écrit. — He wrote to **us**.

In a compound tense it lands before the helper, not before the participle:
«il **l'**a vu», never «il a **l'**vu». The one place it goes after the verb is
a positive command: «regarde-**moi**».

rules.name: «du», «de la», «des» — some, without saying how much
rules.body:
When you're talking about part of something rather than a whole, specific
object, French doesn't leave the noun bare — it puts a small word in front
meaning roughly "some", even in places English drops it entirely.

- Elle achète **du** pain. — She buys (some) bread. «pain» is masculine, so
  «de» plus «le» contracts to «du».
- Elle achète **de la** confiture. — Some jam. «confiture» is feminine, so
  «de la» stays whole.
- Elle achète **des** croissants. — Some croissants. Plural always takes
  «des», whatever the gender.

English can say "bread" and mean some bread. French can't leave the noun on
its own like that — one of «du», «de la», «des» has to be there.

rules.name: A handful of verbs build their past with «être», not «avoir»
rules.body:
Most verbs use «avoir» to build the passé composé. A small set of verbs —
mostly about movement or a change of state, like «aller», «arriver»,
«partir», «rester», «venir» — use «être» instead. When «être» is the helper,
the past participle agrees with the subject, the way an adjective does.

- Ils **sont restés** sous le parapluie. — «restés» because the subject,
  «ils», is plural.
- Elle **est arrivée** à l'heure. — «arrivée» gets an «e» because «elle» is
  feminine.
- Il **a couru**. — «courir» isn't in this set, so it keeps «avoir» and the
  participle never changes shape.

Reflexive verbs — the ones with «se» — always use «être» too, and agree the
same way.

rules.name: The written past — ferma, marcha, partit
rules.body:
French has a past tense that is only ever written: novels, history books,
fairy tales. Nobody speaks it. Where a conversation says «il a fermé», a story
says «il ferma» — same meaning, different register.

- Il **ferma** la porte. — In speech: il a fermé la porte.
- Il **marcha** jusqu'à la gare. — In speech: il a marché.
- Les portes **se fermèrent**. — In speech: elles se sont fermées.

You need to recognise it, not produce it. Most verbs are predictable: -er verbs
end in -a (il parla), and a lot of others end in -it (il partit, il dit).

rules.name: One step further back — avait fait
rules.body:
When a story in the past needs to mention something that happened even earlier,
French uses «avait» or «était» plus the participle. It works exactly like
English "had done".

- Elle ne l'avait pas entendu partir. — He left; her not-hearing came after.
- Il **avait pris** ce train pendant quarante ans. — Before the story starts.
- Il **s'était arrêté** au coin de la rue. — Before he reached the station.

Which helper you use is the same choice as in the passé composé: «être» for
reflexives and for the come-and-go verbs, «avoir» for everything else.

rules.name: «son» and «sa» agree with the thing, not the owner
rules.body:
French possessives take the gender of what is owned. They tell you nothing
about who owns it — «son» is his, her, or its, and only the context decides.

- **son** billet — his ticket or her ticket; «billet» is masculine.
- **sa** femme — his wife; «femme» is feminine.
- **ses** mains — his or her hands; plural.

Before a feminine word starting with a vowel, «sa» becomes «son» for the sound:
«**son** amie» is still a female friend.

rules.name: After a preposition, French uses the infinitive
rules.body:
Where English puts an "-ing" form after a preposition, French puts the plain
dictionary form of the verb.

- **sans** se presser — without hurrying.
- **pour** l'attendre — to wait for him / for waiting for him.
- **avant de** partir — before leaving.

The one exception is «en», which takes the -ant form: «en partant» — while
leaving. Everything else — sans, pour, avant de, après avoir, au lieu de —
takes the infinitive.

rules.name: «en» stands in for «de» plus a thing
rules.body:
«en» replaces a noun introduced by «de», «du», «des», or by a number or
quantity. English usually just leaves the noun out; French insists on marking
the gap.

- Elle **en** mettait deux. — She put out two (of them).
- Tu veux du café ? — J'**en** veux bien. — I'd like some.
- Il **en** revient. — He's coming back from there.

Like other object pronouns it sits in front of the verb, and it stays even when
a number follows: «j'**en** ai trois», never «j'ai trois».

rules.name: «se» when nobody in particular is doing it
rules.body:
French often uses «se» to say something happens, without naming who caused it.
English uses the plain verb, or a passive.

- Les portes **se** fermèrent. — The doors closed.
- Ça **se** dit. — People say that.
- Le vin blanc **se** boit frais. — White wine is drunk chilled.

Without the «se», «les portes fermèrent» would claim the doors closed something
else. The «se» is what turns the action back on the subject.

rules.name: Verbs that act on themselves — se lever, s'arrêter
rules.body:
A lot of everyday French verbs carry a «se». It marks that the subject is also
the target: you lift yourself, you stop yourself. English usually has a
separate word for the same idea and no pronoun at all.

- lever (to lift) → **se lever** — to get up.
- arrêter (to stop something) → **s'arrêter** — to come to a halt.
- presser → **se presser** — to hurry.

The pronoun changes with the subject (je **me** lève, tu **te** lèves), and in
compound tenses these verbs always take «être»: «il **s'était** arrêté».

rules.name: «que» is never optional
rules.body:
English lets you drop "that" when reporting speech or thought. French does not:
the «que» has to be written, and it shortens to «qu'» before a vowel.

- Il dit **qu'**il avait raté le train. — He said (that) he'd missed it.
- Je crois **que** tu as raison. — I think you're right.
- Elle sait **qu'**il ment. — She knows he's lying.

Leaving it out is one of the clearest signs of an English sentence wearing
French words.

rules.name: The standalone pronouns — moi, toi, lui, elle, eux
rules.body:
French has two sets of pronouns. The little ones (le, la, lui, me) can only
live glued to a verb. After a preposition, or standing alone, you need the
strong forms: moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous, eux, elles.

- Le train partait sans **lui**. — Never «sans le».
- Je pense à **elle**. — I'm thinking about her.
- Qui a fait ça ? — **Moi**. — Me.

They're also what you use for emphasis: «**Moi**, je reste» — me, I'm staying.

rules.name: The empty «il» — weather, time, and there-is
rules.body:
Some French sentences need a subject even when nothing is doing anything. «il»
fills the slot and means nothing, just as "it" does in "it's raining".

- **Il** pleuvait encore. — It was still raining.
- **Il** est sept heures. — It's seven o'clock.
- **Il** faut partir. — We have to go.

This «il» never refers to a person, so it is never «elle», whatever the weather
word is.
